```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Forecasts for groups of a population, such as sexes, regions or
deprivation quintiles, are often combined: into totals over the groups,
into gaps between them and into measures of inequality. The uncertainty of
these combinations depends on how the forecasts of the groups move
together. This vignette shows why, describes the two ways in which
mortensor gives forecasts of several groups their dependence, and compares
them on the deprivation quintiles of England.

## Why dependence matters

A forecast is a set of draws, each a possible future of all groups. The
interval of a total comes from the totals of the draws, and the interval
of a gap from the gaps of the draws. For two groups A and B,

* Var(A + B) = Var(A) + Var(B) + 2 Cov(A, B),
* Var(A - B) = Var(A) + Var(B) - 2 Cov(A, B).

The mortality of groups in one country often moves together: medical
progress, epidemics and cold winters reach all of them. Their forecast
errors are then positively correlated. Separate models, one per group, draw the future
of each group independently, so the covariance of their draws is zero.
Totals then get intervals that are too narrow, and gaps get intervals that
are too wide. Where groups move in opposite directions, the covariance is
negative and the errors are reversed: totals get intervals that are too
wide and gaps intervals that are too narrow. The forecast of each group on
its own does not depend on the other groups; dependence matters for
quantities computed from several groups.

## Joint models

Joint models fit all groups together. Their draws carry the dependence of
the model.

* `li_lee()` (Li and Lee 2005): an age pattern and a period index common
  to all groups, and a deviation of each group whose period index follows
  an AR(1) process. The deviations return to their mean over the fitting
  years, so the forecasts of the groups stay together (coherent
  forecasts), and the common index makes them move together.
* `coherent_fdm()` (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013): the product-ratio
  method. The geometric mean of the groups follows a time-series model,
  and the ratio of each group to it is a stationary process.
* `cae()` (Kleinow 2015): the common age effect model. All groups share
  their age effects, and each group has its own period effects, estimated
  with the same weight for every group. Kleinow (2015) does not forecast.
  In mortensor the period effects of all groups follow one random walk with
  drift whose innovations are correlated between the groups (a
  package-specific choice, see `?cae`). Each group keeps its own drift, so
  the forecasts of the groups can drift apart.

## Coupling separate forecasts

Sometimes a separate model per group gives the best forecast of each
group, but its draws are independent. Ensemble copula coupling (ECC;
Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting 2013) keeps the forecast of each
cell (an age, a year and a group) of such a base model and takes the
dependence from the draws of a joint model, the template. In each cell
the values of the base model are sorted and handed to the draws in the
order of the template: the draw in which the template is lowest receives
the lowest value of the base model, and so on. Five draws of one cell:

```{r}
base <- c(0.012, 0.010, 0.011, 0.014, 0.013)
template <- c(0.021, 0.025, 0.019, 0.022, 0.020)
sort(base)[rank(template)]
```

Each cell keeps exactly the values of the base model. The draws as a
whole take the ranks of the template, between groups, between ages and
between years. `coupled(lee_carter(), template = cae())` couples inside a
model, `reconciled(..., dependence = "ecc", template = cae())` couples
before reconciling, and `mt_couple()` couples two sets of forecast draws.

## Example: deprivation quintiles in England

Deaths and populations by sex and deprivation quintile (`ons_data`), at
ages 50 and over. Q1 is the most deprived quintile. The totals are England
by sex.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
x <- mt_subset(x, ages = c(50, Inf))
h <- mt_hierarchy(quintile = list(total = "England"))
```

`cae()` needs more years than age groups (Kleinow 2015, Section 2). The
nine age groups from 50 leave room for training windows of ten years and
more. The number of common age effects (`order`) and whether women and men
share them (`common_by`) can be chosen by the approximate BIC of Kleinow
(2015, eq. 5):

```{r}
bic <- CJ(order = 1:3, common_by = c("none", "sex"))
bic[, bic := mapply(function(p, cb) {
  mt_fit(cae(order = p, common_by = if (cb == "none") NULL else cb), x)$fits$bic
}, order, common_by)]
bic
```

One common age effect for both sexes has the lowest BIC. The correlations
of the innovations of the period effects between the quintiles of women:

```{r}
fit_cae <- mt_fit(cae(), x)
cr <- mt_parameters(fit_cae)[parameter == "cor_kappa1" & grepl("female", stratum) & grepl("female", index)]
dcast(cr[, .(stratum, index, value = round(value, 2))], stratum ~ index)
```

The quintiles move together: in a year in which the mortality of one
quintile falls more than its trend, that of the others mostly does too.

### Forecasts

Four models, each with the totals for England as the sums of the quintiles
in every draw (`method = "bottom_up"`), so that the totals show the
dependence of the parts:

* **separate**: a Lee-Carter model for each group;
* **CAE**: the common age effect model;
* **ECC**: the Lee-Carter models of each group, coupled to the CAE model;
* **Li-Lee**: the Li-Lee model with a common factor for each sex.

```{r}
specs <- list(
  separate = reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "bottom_up"),
  CAE = reconciled(cae(), h, method = "bottom_up"),
  ECC = reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "bottom_up", dependence = "ecc", template = cae()),
  "Li-Lee" = reconciled(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), h, method = "bottom_up"))
fcs <- lapply(specs, function(s) mt_forecast(mt_fit(s, x), to = 2030, n_draws = 500, seed = 1))
```

The correlation between the paths of life expectancy at 50 of women in Q1
and Q5 in 2030:

```{r}
e50 <- lapply(fcs, life_expectancy, at = 50, paths = TRUE)
round(sapply(e50, function(e) cor(e["2030", "female.Q1", ], e["2030", "female.Q5", ])), 2)
```

Life expectancy at 50 in 2030, median and 95% interval, for women in Q1
and Q5 and in England:

```{r}
mt_compare_forecasts(fcs, periods = 2030, at = 50, strata = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5", "female.England"),
                     digits = 2)
```

Life expectancy at 50 in 2030 for England, the sum of the quintiles:

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_compare(fcs, at = 50, strata = c("female.England", "male.England"), periods = 2030)
```

The observed gap in life expectancy at 50 between Q1 and Q5 widened:

```{r}
e_obs <- life_expectancy(mt_array(x, "deaths") / mt_array(x, "exposure"), mt_grid(x)$age, at = 50)
yrs <- c("2001", "2010", "2019")
round(e_obs[yrs, c("female.Q1", "male.Q1")] - e_obs[yrs, c("female.Q5", "male.Q5")], 2)
```

The forecast gap in 2030, path by path:

```{r}
gap <- rbindlist(lapply(names(fcs), function(n) {
  g <- mt_contrast(fcs[[n]], var = "quintile", ref = "Q5", at = 50)
  cbind(model = n, g[period == 2030 & level == "Q1", .(sex, q0.025, q0.5, q0.975)])
}))
gap[, width := q0.975 - q0.025]
gap[, (3:6) := lapply(.SD, round, 2), .SDcols = 3:6]
gap
```

Separate models draw the quintiles independently: the correlation of
their paths is close to zero. With CAE and ECC it is about 0.8, with Li-Lee
0.94. ECC keeps the forecast of each quintile from the Lee-Carter models,
so Q1 and Q5 have the same intervals as with the separate models; the
totals and the gaps change. The 95% interval of the life expectancy of
women in England is 1.5 years wide with separate models, 2.3 years with
CAE, 3.0 years with ECC and 5.2 years with Li-Lee. For the gap between Q1
and Q5 the separate models give the widest interval: 5.5 years for women,
against 2.1 to 2.8 years with the other three. Li-Lee
forecasts a smaller gap than the other models, because its deviations
return towards their mean over the fitting years.

### Backtests

Forecasts from the origins 2010 to 2014, five years ahead, scored against
the observed rates and life expectancy at 50, and against the gaps in
life expectancy between each quintile and Q5 (`contrast`). The data hold
the totals, so that they are scored too.

```{r}
xa <- mt_aggregate_strata(x, h)
bt <- mt_compare(specs, xa, origins = 2010:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy",
                 contrast = c(var = "quintile", ref = "Q5"))
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov80", "cov95"), hierarchy = h, targets = c("rate", "life_expectancy"))
```

The columns ending in `_le` score life expectancy at 50. `bottom` are the
quintiles by sex and `total` England by sex. The gap between Q1 and Q5:

```{r}
mt_score_table(bt[quintile == "Q1"], metrics = c("crps", "cov50", "cov80", "cov95"),
               targets = "life_expectancy_gap")
```

The quintiles (`bottom`) are forecast equally well by the separate models
and by ECC (CRPS 0.0378), because ECC keeps the forecast of each cell; the
small differences in coverage come from the Poisson variation of the
deaths, which is drawn after the coupling. CAE (0.0396) and Li-Lee
(0.0415) forecast the quintiles less accurately than the Lee-Carter
models.

The totals show the effect of the dependence. With separate models, the
95% intervals for England contain 41% of the observed rates and 30% of the
observed life expectancies at 50: sums of independent parts vary too
little. With CAE they contain 63% and 62%, with ECC 65% and 68%, and with
Li-Lee 74% and 76%. ECC has the lowest CRPS for the totals. Every model
stays below 95%, as in the vignette "Coherent forecasts: totals and their
parts": mortality improved more slowly after 2011 than in the training
years.

The gap between Q1 and Q5 shows the other side. The intervals of the
separate models are too wide: their 50% intervals contain 94% of the
observed gaps. CAE (38%) and ECC (52%) come closer to 50%, and ECC has the
lowest CRPS. Li-Lee forecasts the gap to return towards its mean over the
fitting years, while the observed gap widened (see above); the 95%
intervals of Li-Lee contain 16% of the observed gaps.

Each score of the totals and of the gap rests on 50 values per model (two
sexes, five origins, five horizons) from overlapping forecasts. The
results describe these data and years; for other data, a backtest of the
totals and gaps that matter shows which method suits them.

## Choosing a method

* For totals and gaps, use draws that carry the dependence between the
  groups: a joint model, or separate models coupled to one.
* ECC keeps the forecast of each cell from the base model and takes how
  groups, ages and years move together from the template; check the
  template's dependence in a backtest of totals and gaps, as above.
* A joint model whose deviations return to their mean over the fitting
  years, such as `li_lee()`, forecasts gaps that return towards their past
  level; where gaps are widening, check this in a backtest.

## References

Hyndman RJ, Booth H, Yasmeen F (2013). Coherent mortality forecasting: the
product-ratio method with functional time series models. *Demography*
50(1): 261-283.

Kleinow T (2015). A common age effect model for the mortality of multiple
populations. *Insurance: Mathematics and Economics* 63: 147-152.

Li N, Lee R (2005). Coherent mortality forecasts for a group of
populations: an extension of the Lee-Carter method. *Demography* 42(3):
575-594.

Schefzik R, Thorarinsdottir TL, Gneiting T (2013). Uncertainty
quantification in complex simulation models using ensemble copula
coupling. *Statistical Science* 28(4): 616-640.
